title: What a package manager is for
summary: Installing software by hand leaves you alone with its libraries, its updates and its removal. A package manager tracks all of that, from repositories it can check.

scheme: who updates it when a flaw is found?
which files to delete to remove it?
sudo dnf install nginx    (Rocky, Red Hat)
text: You need the nginx web server on a server. You could download it from a website, unpack it and copy its files into place.
Then come the three questions on the left.
A package manager answers them for you.

scheme: every file, and which package owns it
text: A package is a program with a label: its files, its version, and the packages it needs (its dependencies).
- apt or dnf fetches it from a repository, with its dependencies.
- It records every file it installs, to remove them later (apt remove keeps settings files, apt purge doesn't).
- apt update then apt upgrade, or dnf upgrade, updates every package at once, security fixes included.

scheme: packages ──signed by the distro──▶ apt, dnf
text: Why trust what comes down? Everything is signed by the distribution: Debian signs the repository's list, which holds a checksum of every package; Rocky signs each package.
- apt and dnf check that signature with a key they already trust.
- They refuse a package that doesn't match.

scheme: runs a script you haven't read, as root
may bypass apt/dnf: no updates, no removal
✔ else a vendor you trust: its repo, its key
text: Some READMEs say: pipe this download into sudo bash. That runs a script from the internet as root before you can read it. It may copy files the package manager never hears of, or add a repository and a key you never chose.
- Look in your distribution first, then in its official extras: backports on Debian, EPEL on Rocky.
- Else, add the vendor's repository with its signing key. Only for a vendor you trust: every update it ships runs as root.
